candidateSources.sourceLocator: OpenStax University Physics Vol.1 (via Physics LibreTexts), §5.5 'Mass and Weight', Eq. 5.9
candidateSources.retrievedPassage: "w = mg" (Eq. 5.9), where w is weight (the gravitational force acting on an object), m is mass, and g is acceleration due to gravity; applies "when the net external force on an object is its weight"; on Earth g = 9.80 m/s², so "the weight of a 1.00-kg object on Earth is 9.80 N"; weight varies with location because g does, while mass does not.

normalizedClaims.claimText: Weight w equals mass m times gravitational acceleration g (w = mg); this applies when the net external force on an object is its weight; on Earth g = 9.80 m/s², so a 1.00 kg mass weighs 9.80 N, and weight (unlike mass) varies with location because g does.

candidateSources.sourceLocator: Workforce LibreTexts, 'Trigonometry and Single Phase AC Generation for Electricians' (Flinn), §3.5 'Frequency and Alternators'
candidateSources.retrievedPassage: "f = (P/2) × (N/60)" and equivalently "f = PN/120", where "f = frequency in hertz", "P = number of poles", "N = rotational speed in RPM"; "We divide the number of poles by two because there will always be a set of two poles" and "We divide the RPM by 60 because we are concerned with rotations per second, not rotations per minute."

normalizedClaims.claimText: An alternator's output frequency f (Hz) equals half the number of poles P times the rotational speed N (in RPM) divided by 60 -- f = (P/2)×(N/60), equivalently f = PN/120 -- because a full electrical cycle occurs for every pair of poles passed and RPM must be converted to revolutions per second; this is a mathematically equivalent form of f = (pole pairs) × (rotational speed in rev/s).

claimDimensionBindings.claimText: An alternator's output frequency f (Hz) equals half the number of poles P times the rotational speed N (in RPM) divided by 60 -- f = (P/2)×(N/60), equivalently f = PN/120 -- because a full electrical cycle occurs for every pair of poles passed and RPM must be converted to revolutions per second; this is a mathematically equivalent form of f = (pole pairs) × (rotational speed in rev/s).

candidateSources.sourceLocator: Georgia Tech Physics Book, 'Charging and Discharging a Capacitor', https://physicsbook.gatech.edu/Charging_and_Discharging_a_Capacitor
candidateSources.retrievedPassage: "A capacitor is a two-conductor device that stores energy in the electric field between its plates." "When you connect an uncharged capacitor to a battery through a resistor, charge piles up on the plates over time — that's charging. Disconnect the battery and let the capacitor drive current through a resistor, and the stored charge bleeds back off — that's discharging." "A capacitor is not a battery. A battery maintains a roughly constant emf from chemistry; a capacitor's voltage rises or falls as charge moves on or off its plates."

normalizedClaims.claimText: A capacitor is a two-conductor device that stores energy in the electric field between its plates; connecting an uncharged capacitor to a battery through a resistor causes charge to pile up on the plates over time (charging), while disconnecting the battery and driving current through a resistor lets the stored charge bleed back off (discharging) -- unlike a battery, whose voltage stays roughly constant from chemistry, a capacitor's voltage rises or falls as charge moves onto or off its plates.

claimDimensionBindings.claimText: A capacitor is a two-conductor device that stores energy in the electric field between its plates; connecting an uncharged capacitor to a battery through a resistor causes charge to pile up on the plates over time (charging), while disconnecting the battery and driving current through a resistor lets the stored charge bleed back off (discharging) -- unlike a battery, whose voltage stays roughly constant from chemistry, a capacitor's voltage rises or falls as charge moves onto or off its plates.

candidateSources.sourceLocator: Littelfuse (Teccor brand Thyristors), Application Note AN1001 'Fundamental Characteristics of Thyristors', p.2, §'Triac → Basic Operation'
candidateSources.retrievedPassage: "Its primary function is to control power bilaterally in an AC circuit." "Operation of a Triac can be related to two SCRs connected in parallel in opposite directions." "Although the gates are shown separately for each SCR, a Triac has a single gate and can be triggered by either polarity." "Since a Triac operates in both directions, it behaves essentially the same in either direction as an SCR would behave in the forward direction (blocking or operating)."

normalizedClaims.claimText: A TRIAC's primary function is to control power bilaterally (in both directions) in an AC circuit; its operation is equivalent to two silicon-controlled rectifiers (SCRs) connected in parallel in opposite directions, but unlike two separate SCRs a TRIAC has a single gate terminal that can be triggered by either polarity, and because it operates in both directions it behaves, in either direction, essentially the same as an SCR would behave in its forward (blocking or conducting) direction.

claimDimensionBindings.claimText: A TRIAC's primary function is to control power bilaterally (in both directions) in an AC circuit; its operation is equivalent to two silicon-controlled rectifiers (SCRs) connected in parallel in opposite directions, but unlike two separate SCRs a TRIAC has a single gate terminal that can be triggered by either polarity, and because it operates in both directions it behaves, in either direction, essentially the same as an SCR would behave in its forward (blocking or conducting) direction.

candidateSources.sourceLocator: AT&T Bell System Practices, Plant Series, Section 502-200-100, Issue 3 (March 1964), §2.01(a) and §2.09/Fig. 8
candidateSources.retrievedPassage: "531A: For use as a high impedance extension ringer. Consists of a B-type ringer and an 0.5-uf capacitor." Fig. 8 ('687A Subscriber Set, Internal View') labels a '198C CAPACITOR' wired directly alongside the 'C4A RINGER' inside the subscriber set assembly.

normalizedClaims.claimText: In AT&T Bell System subscriber telephone sets, the ringer is standardly provided as an integral paired combination with a dedicated capacitor -- for example, the 531A high-impedance extension-ringer set 'consists of a B-type ringer and an 0.5-uf capacitor', and the internal assembly of the 685-, 686-, 687-, and 690-type subscriber sets wires a 198C capacitor directly to the C4A ringer -- documenting the capacitor as a standard component of the ringer circuit in the telephone operating company's own official engineering practice for these sets.
